summary: Polymorphism means 'many forms'. One superclass/interface reference can point to objects of different subclasses, and each object runs its **own** overridden method.

Binding connects a method call to a method body. **Static (early)** binding happens at compile time: overload choice, and `private`/`final`/`static` methods. **Dynamic (late)** binding happens at run time, using the **actual object type**.

Casting: upcasting (subclass to superclass) is automatic and safe. Downcasting needs an explicit cast. It compiles, but throws `ClassCastException` at run time if the object isn't really that type. Use `instanceof` to check first.
The **reference (declared) type** decides what compiles. The **object type** decides which overridden method runs.
The benefits of polymorphism are exactly **Simplicity** and **Extensibility**. LSP (Liskov, 1988): subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.

The slides' **three ways of method overriding**: 1) a subclass overrides a superclass method, 2) a subclass implements the abstract methods of an abstract class, 3) a concrete class implements the methods of an interface.
mustMemorise: Polymorphism = 'many forms' (Greek). Overriding is the necessary tool for it.
Static binding = early = **compile time**. Dynamic binding = late = **run time** (based on the actual object).
Java uses dynamic binding for all methods EXCEPT `private`, `final` and `static` methods.
Overloading is resolved by static binding (on the declared argument types). Overriding is resolved by dynamic binding (on the object type).
`<reference type> name = new <Object Type>()`: the reference type is checked at **compile time**, the object type at **run time**.
Upcast `Shape s = new Rectangle();` is OK. `Rectangle r = s;` is a COMPILE error. `Rectangle r = (Rectangle) s;` compiles, but throws ClassCastException at run time if `s` is not really a Rectangle.
Calling a subclass-only method through a superclass variable is a **compile error** (e.g. `Object st = new String(); st.charAt(0);`).
`x instanceof C` is true if x is a C or any **descendant** of C. `null instanceof C` is false.
LSP: Barbara **Liskov**, **1988**. 'Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.'
The 3 ways of overriding: (1) subclass overrides superclass, (2) implementing abstract methods of an abstract class, (3) a concrete class implementing an interface's methods.
Dynamic binding works even inside a superclass **constructor**. The subclass override runs before the subclass's fields are initialised, so they are still `0`/`null`.

items.title: Polymorphism definition
notes: Polymorphism means **'many forms'** (Greek).
In OOP it is the ability of an **object reference** to refer to different types. Which method runs depends on where the object sits in the inheritance hierarchy.
Overriding is a **necessary tool** for polymorphism. The subclass method may **replace** or **refine** the parent's method.

items.title: Refine vs replace (labels are confusing)
notes: **Refine** = call `super.printInfo()` and then add more. That is the version in the slide text: `Employee details are :` → `super.printInfo()` → salary.
**Replace** = rewrite the method without calling `super`. That is the version visible in the image (prints `Employee name is :` …).
In the image, the '// refine' comment sits beside the *replace* body because of an animation overlay. Go by the rule: uses `super` = refine.

items.title: Animal / Eagle / Tiger / Shark
notes: The hollow triangle at Animal means the three subclasses inherit from it, and each **overrides** `move()`.
With one variable `Animal animal`, reassigning it to `new Eagle()`, then `new Tiger()`, then `new Shark()` makes `animal.move()` run Eagle's, then Tiger's, then Shark's `move()`.

items.title: Polymorphism via a superclass variable
notes: When you call a method through a superclass variable, the **subclass version** runs, chosen by the type of the **object** the variable refers to. The slide's wording 'type of the reference' is corrected on the slide to 'object'.
The same name and signature can cause different actions depending on the object's type.
This lets you add new classes with **minimal modification** to existing code: `call(Animal a)` works for any future subclass.

items.title: Liskov Substitution Principle
notes: By **Barbara Liskov, 1988**. If replacing o2 (type T) with o1 (type S) leaves the behaviour of every program P written for T **unchanged**, then S is a subtype of T.
Paraphrase to memorise: **'Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.'**
Being able to substitute requires the *behaviour* to be unchanged, not just that the code compiles (more in Ch9).

items.title: Static vs dynamic binding
notes: Binding = connecting a **method call** to a **method body**.
**Static / early** binding: bound at **compile time**. **Dynamic / late** binding: delayed until **execution time (runtime)**, based on the **actual object** referred to.
Trap: `Shape circle = new Circle();` is placed under 'static binding', but `circle.print()` is dynamically bound and runs Circle's `print()`. The compiler only checks that Shape *has* a `print()`.

items.title: Reference type vs object type
notes: Java uses dynamic binding **by default**: the **object type** (actual type), not the declared/reference type, decides which method runs.
Synonyms: reference type = declared type = variable type. Object type = the class after `new`.
`Object anObj = new Person();` has reference type Object and object type Person. An interface can be the reference type: `IAnimal a = new Cat();`.

items.title: Static binding: overload chosen by declared type
notes: `Collection c = new HashSet(); et.sort(c);` prints **`Inside Collection sort method`** (verified).
Overload resolution uses the **declared** type of the argument (Collection) at compile time, even though the object is a HashSet.
Contrast: for overriding, the run-time object type decides.

items.title: Dynamic binding: Vehicle v = new Car()
notes: `vehicle.start()` prints **`Inside start method of Car`**: the method is overridden, so the object type (Car) wins.
Bus is never created, so its `start()` never runs.

items.title: What is NOT dynamically bound
notes: Java uses dynamic binding for all methods **except `private`, `final` and `static`**. Those are bound statically, because they cannot be overridden.
A `static` method with the same signature in a subclass **hides** the parent's method instead of overriding it. The reference type decides which one runs.
Dynamic binding lets a base-class method call methods whose details are defined later in subclasses: 'program in the general'.
Also verified: if a superclass constructor calls an overridden method, the **subclass** version runs, and it sees subclass fields still at `0`/`null`.

items.title: Sale.lessThan calls bill() dynamically
notes: Inside `Sale.lessThan`, both `bill()` and `otherSale.bill()` are dynamically bound, so `discount.bill()` runs **DiscountSale's** version: 11 × 0.9 = 9.9.
`simple.lessThan(discount)` checks 10 < 9.9, which is false, so `!false` prints `code can still be compiled!`.
Typo: `new sale(...)` should be `new Sale(...)` (Java is case-sensitive), and the slide uses curly quotes.

items.title: Upcasting
notes: Upcasting = assigning a derived-class object to a base-class (or any ancestor) variable. It is **implicit** and always safe.
`shape.findArea()` runs **Rectangle's** `findArea()` because of dynamic binding.
`shape.getWidth()` would NOT compile, because Shape has no getWidth. Typo: `new Rectangle(15,10));` has an extra `)`.

items.title: Downcasting, plus the 'int height' bug
notes: `Rectangle rect = shape;` without a cast is a **compile error**.

`Rectangle rect = (Rectangle) shape;` with `shape = new Shape()` **compiles**, but throws **ClassCastException** at run time (verified). The compiler only checks that the types are related, and the real object is checked at run time.
Slide bug: `int height = rect.getHeight(); // compiler OK`. Since `getHeight()` returns `double`, this is actually a compile error ('possible lossy conversion', verified).
Exam: the slide's intended point is that a subclass method through a subclass reference compiles. For a literal `int = double` line, answer 'compile error'.

items.title: Downcasting is the programmer's responsibility
notes: The compiler does **not** check whether a downcast makes sense.
A downcast that doesn't make sense usually gives a **run-time error** (ClassCastException).

items.title: instanceof
notes: Downcasting is only sensible if the object really is an instance of the target type. Check with `object instanceof ClassName`.
It is true if the object is of that class **or any descendant**, so `personObj instanceof Object` is always true for a non-null object.
`null instanceof X` is **false** (verified). That is why the `equals` pattern needs no separate null check.

items.title: equals(Object) uses instanceof + downcast
notes: Pattern: null → false. If `!(anObject instanceof Person)` → false. Otherwise downcast with `(Person) anObject` and compare fields.
`instanceof Person` also accepts a **Student** (subclass). The commented-out `getClass() != anObject.getClass()` requires the exact same class.
`Object anObject = new String("Tom"); (Person) anObject` compiles but throws ClassCastException at run time. That is why you check first.

items.title: Cylinder/Figure: compile vs runtime checks
notes: The outer Cylinder circle contains the inner Figure circle: a Cylinder object has all of Figure's members plus `getHeight`/`getRadius`.

`Figure fig = new Cylinder(); fig.getArea();` passes compile and run time. `Cylinder cy = fig;` is compile NOK. `(Cylinder) fig` on a real `new Figure()` is compile OK, runtime NOK. `cy.getHeight()` compiles.
**The reference type is used to check at compile time. The object type is used to check at run time.**
The red X on `#getCenterGravity()` means a protected member is not accessible from an outside (non-subclass, other-package) client.

items.title: Allowed assignments (the 4 rules)
notes: Superclass ref to superclass var: OK (`Object ob = new Object()`). Subclass ref to subclass var: OK (`String st = new String()`).
Subclass to superclass var: **safe** (is-a), `Object st = new String()`. But `st.charAt(0)` is a **compile error**, because subclass-only members aren't visible through a superclass variable.

Superclass to subclass var: **compile error** (`String ob = new Object()`). An explicit cast `(String) new Object()` compiles, but **throws ClassCastException at run time** (verified). The slide shows it in green, but it only gets past the compiler.
A cast between **unrelated** classes (e.g. `(Q) p`, where P and Q are siblings) is a **compile error** (verified).

items.title: Benefit 1: Simplicity
notes: Code dealing with a family of types can ignore type-specific details and just use the **base type**.
The object may actually be the base class or any subclass. This makes code easier to write and to understand.

items.title: Benefit 2: Extensibility
notes: You add new functionality by creating **new subclasses** of an off-the-shelf base class **without modifying** the base class or the other subclasses.
The benefits are exactly 2: **Simplicity** and **Extensibility**.

items.title: ShapeApp code is broken as written
notes: Bugs: Circle's constructor is named `Rectangle(double r)` (compile error), `shapes` is used before it is declared, `shapes[1] = …` uses array syntax on an ArrayList, the `println(` is missing its `)`, and it uses curly quotes.
Intended idea: `ArrayList<Shape> shapes` holding Circles/Rectangles, then `for (Shape s : shapes) s.area()` runs each object's own `area()`.
Exam: take away the polymorphic loop, not the literal code.

items.title: THE three ways of method overriding
notes: 1) **Method overriding**: methods of a subclass override the methods of a superclass.
2) **Overriding (implementation) of abstract methods**: methods of a subclass implement the abstract methods of an **abstract class**.
3) **Overriding (implementation) through the Java interface**: methods of a **concrete class** implement the methods of the **interface**.
Don't mix this up with Ch3's **2 ways** (Refinement / Replacement), which describe *how* a single override is written.

items.title: CareTaker.takeAWalk(IAnimal pet)
notes: `ct.takeAWalk(cat)` prints `Cat moves....` then `Meow !`. `ct.takeAWalk(lion)` prints `Lion moves...` then `ROAR !`.
The parameter type is the **interface** IAnimal. Any class that implements it can be passed. This is way 3 of overriding.

items.title: Overloading = static binding, interface parameter = dynamic binding
notes: Writing `takeAWalk(Cat)`, `takeAWalk(Lion)`, … is **method overloading**: the method is chosen at **compile time** (static binding), and you need a new method for every new animal.
One `takeAWalk(IAnimal pet)`: which object implements IAnimal is known only at **run time**, so this is **dynamic binding**. New animals (Dog, Elephant, Tiger) need no change to CareTaker.

items.title: LivingThings / Mammal / Dog
notes: `Mammal` does not implement the abstract `speak()`, so it **must be abstract**. `Dog` is concrete: it implements `speak()`, overrides `move()`/`grow()`, and inherits `eat()`.
`Mammal m = new Dog(); m.speak();` compiles because Mammal inherits the abstract `speak()` declaration. At run time it runs Dog's.

The red 'static' labels ask 'what if move() were static?' (verified): if both are static, `m.move()` prints `Mammal move!` (hiding, chosen by the reference type). If only one of them is static, it's a compile error.

items.title: Program output text doesn't match the code
notes: The slide shows `Dog moves!`, `Mammal eats!`, `Dog grows!`. The code actually prints `Dog move!`, `Mammal eat!`, `Dog grow!` (verified).
Real output, twice (for `mDog` and for `m`): `Woof!` / `Dog move!` / `Mammal eat!` / `Dog grow!`. The same result both times = dynamic binding.
Exam: the pattern (Dog's speak/move/grow, Mammal's eat) is what matters. Use the exact strings in the code.

items.title: Summary
notes: Polymorphism = 'many forms'. LSP = subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.
Benefits = simplicity and extensibility. A downcast that makes no sense gives a run-time error.
